task.title: Study Forensics: Houseplants and depression scores (synthetic)
task.prompt: A cross-sectional survey of 5,000 remote workers asked participants how many houseplants they owned and assessed their depressive symptoms with a standard questionnaire. Those with five or more houseplants reported average depression scores 30 percent lower than those with no plants. The article concludes that "bringing the outdoors in" can improve mental health and urges employers to reimburse plant purchases for home offices. No experimental design is used, and the survey authors acknowledge that plant owners also tended to have higher incomes, more natural light and more leisure time.
task.context:
The synthetic summary equates owning multiple houseplants with improved mental health
based on a cross-sectional survey, ignoring socioeconomic confounders.
task.reference_solution: The synthetic summary equates owning multiple houseplants with improved mental health based on a cross-sectional survey, ignoring socioeconomic confounders. The recommendation for employers to subsidise plants is unsupported by causal evidence.

functional_descriptions: no causal inference is possible from a cross-sectional design
the observed association may be driven by confounding variables
the article makes causal claims from correlational data

common_errors: accepting the causal claim at face value
treating the policy recommendation as evidence-based
task.diagnostic_focus: Can the agent identify correlation-as-causation and confounder blindness?
task.gold_summary: The synthetic summary equates owning multiple houseplants with improved mental health based on a cross-sectional survey, ignoring socioeconomic confounders. The recommendation for employers to subsidise plants is unsupported by causal evidence.

gold_evidence_spans.span: bringing the outdoors in can improve mental health
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Asserts a causal relationship without evidence.

gold_evidence_spans.span: urges employers to reimburse plant purchases
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Generalises to policy based on correlation.

gold_evidence_spans.span: plant owners also tended to have higher incomes, more natural light and more leisure time
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Indicates confounders the article fails to control for.

task.gold_justification:
Cross-sectional survey with no experimental design. The article makes a causal claim
('bringing the outdoors in can improve mental health') and a policy recommendation
(reimburse plant purchases) from correlational data with acknowledged confounders
(income, natural light, leisure time). Textbook correlation-as-causation.
task.gold_alternative_reading:
No strong alternative. The causal claim is explicit, the confounders are acknowledged
but not controlled, and the policy recommendation has no evidential basis. Even a
charitable reading cannot justify the causal leap.
task.curator_notes:
Easiest case in the pilot set. All models get the label right in both sprints.
Finding recall is low (33%) because expected_findings includes mechanism_not_demonstrated,
which is debatable for a survey study. Consider removing mechanism_not_demonstrated
from expected_findings in future revision — the core issue is correlation, not mechanism.
